passage:
Ivan chose lunch in Lisbon the way he always did: two seconds at the café counter, "the soup, please," done. Same with which tram to catch or what to wear to class. Familiar ground, small stakes; the gut was fine.
The two-year lease on the flat above the bakery was another matter. The landlord wanted a signature by the weekend, and the flat was bright and lovely. Ivan felt the pull.
Instead he printed a checklist: rent against his part-time wages, the notice period, the damp patch in the bathroom. He slept on it twice. On Saturday he showed it to Beatriz, a friend who had rented for years.
"Ask them to fix the damp in writing," she said. "And check the break clause."
Ivan did both before signing on Monday.

qa.q: What did Ivan order at the café counter?
qa.a: The soup.

qa.q: Why was Ivan happy to decide lunch in two seconds but not the lease?
qa.a: Lunch is familiar and small, so his gut is good enough; a two-year lease is big and hard to undo, so the pull of the bright flat needed checking.

qa.q: Which tools did Ivan use for the big decision?
qa.a: A printed checklist, sleeping on it twice, and advice from Beatriz, who had rented for years.

qa.q: How might the landlord see Ivan's requests?
qa.a: The landlord might find them a little fussy, but would likely see a careful tenant who will be reliable.

grounding: A young man decides everyday things by gut but uses a checklist, sleep and a friend's advice for a two-year lease.

passage:
In the university mess, Rehana picked her tray in the time it took to say "rajma rice". Same with her seat in lectures or her library corner. Small, familiar choices; no need to agonise.
Switching from engineering to design was different. One bad week in the coding lab had made her want to fill in the transfer form that same afternoon.
She didn't. She wrote a checklist instead: fees, the lost year, her portfolio, what she actually enjoyed. She slept on it for a week. Then she booked a slot with Zainab, the student advisor in the academic office.
Zainab read the list. "Is it design you want, or getting away from one bad week?"
Rehana thought. "Both, maybe. Can I sit in on a design class first?"
Zainab signed a visitor pass.

qa.q: What did Rehana want to do after the bad week in the coding lab?
qa.a: Fill in the transfer form that same afternoon.

qa.q: What was Rehana feeling unsure about when Zainab asked her question?
qa.a: Whether she truly wanted design or mainly wanted to escape one bad week; she admits it might be both.

qa.q: Why did Rehana's slow approach suit this choice?
qa.a: A course switch is big and costly to undo, so a checklist, a week of sleep, advice and a trial class fit better than the quick gut she uses for lunch.

qa.q: How might Zainab view Rehana's checklist?
qa.a: Zainab probably sees a student taking a big decision seriously, which makes it easy to help with one sharp question.

grounding: A student trusts quick instinct for mess and seating choices but slows down with a checklist, sleep and advice before switching courses.

passage:
Dear Lakshmi Mashi,

You told me at the wedding to trust my gut, and I've been thinking about when that works.

For small things it's perfect. I pick my train compartment, my lunch, which assignment to do first, all by feel, and I'm usually right because I've done them a hundred times.

But the scholarship offer from Hyderabad isn't small. It means leaving Kolkata, a new language, and a bond to teach for two years afterwards. My gut screamed yes the second I read it.

So I did it the slow way. A checklist of what I'd gain and lose. Three nights' sleep. A call with a senior who took the same scholarship last year.

The answer is still yes, but now I know why, and I know about the bond.

Love,
Bidisha

qa.q: How many nights did Bidisha sleep on the scholarship decision?
qa.a: Three nights.

qa.q: Why does Bidisha trust gut feeling for lunch and train compartments?
qa.a: Bidisha has done them a hundred times, so quick feelings are usually right and little is lost if they're not.

qa.q: What did the slow way add, even though the answer stayed yes?
qa.a: It brought the two-year teaching bond into view and gave clear reasons, so the choice is made knowingly, not on excitement alone.

qa.q: How might Lakshmi Mashi feel reading this letter?
qa.a: Lakshmi Mashi might feel proud that the advice was taken thoughtfully, and reassured that such a big step was checked. 😊

grounding: A student explains using gut feeling for routine choices and a checklist, sleep and a senior's advice for a big scholarship decision.

passage: Farhan, you asked for my college radio segment, so here's my system. Amma calls me her two-second girl. Small, familiar stuff, I go with my gut. What to eat at the canteen, which shirt, which bus: two seconds, done. If it's wrong, I lose nothing. Last month was different. My department offered me a switch from mechanical engineering to product design. It was exciting, and my gut said yes, instantly. But you can't undo two years. So I slowed right down. I made a checklist: what I'd lose, what I'd gain, what the design seniors actually do all day. I slept on it three nights. I sat with two seniors and my old maths teacher. On the fourth morning I still said yes, but calmly, knowing why. I'm Ganga, and the gut still gets a vote, just not the only one on big days.

qa.q: How many nights did Ganga sleep on the decision?
qa.a: Three nights.

qa.q: Why did Ganga slow down even though her gut said yes instantly?
qa.a: She knew the switch could not be undone, so she wanted to be sure the excited feeling was backed by facts.

qa.q: Which of Ganga's steps could someone use for any big, new choice?
qa.a: Making a checklist of gains and losses, sleeping on it for a few nights, and talking to people who know that path.

qa.q: How might the design seniors have felt when Ganga came to ask questions?
qa.a: They were probably glad to help and to be taken seriously, since she wanted to know what they actually do all day.

grounding: A young adult trusts quick gut choices for small familiar matters and slows down with checklists, sleep and advice for a big one.

passage: I'm Hansa, and I've shared a flat with Arohi in Indore for a year. She's the fastest decider I know. At the tea stall she says "cutting, less sugar" before the man even looks up. She picks her kurta in the morning without opening the cupboard fully. So I was surprised last month when a colleague offered her a puppy. She didn't say yes. She wrote a list on the fridge: who walks it, who pays the vet, what happens when we travel, what the landlord says. She slept on it for a week. She called her brother, and a friend who fosters dogs. She even stood outside the building at 6 a.m. to see if she'd really get up. I don't know what she was feeling inside. But on the eighth day she said, "Not yet, maybe next year." She seemed at peace.

qa.q: What did Arohi order at the tea stall?
qa.a: "Cutting, less sugar."

qa.q: What might Arohi have been thinking when she stood outside at 6 a.m.?
qa.a: She seemed to want to test honestly whether she could keep up with a dog's needs, rather than trusting how cute the puppy felt.

qa.q: What made Arohi's approach to the puppy wise?
qa.a: She matched the effort to the stakes: quick for tea and clothes, but lists, time, advice and a real test for a big, lasting commitment.

qa.q: How does Hansa see Arohi's slow decision, given how fast Arohi usually is?
qa.a: Hansa was surprised, and could not know Arohi's inner feelings, but noticed she seemed at peace with her choice.

grounding: A flatmate watches a young adult decide small things instantly but slow down with lists, sleep and advice for a big one.
